question.worked_solution:
First, note that the denominator's conjugate is $\sqrt{x-3}-\sqrt{x-2}.$

Now, to rationalize the denominator, we multiply both the numerator and denominator by the conjugate $\sqrt{x-3}-\sqrt{x-2},$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{x-3}+\sqrt{x-2}} & = \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{x-3}+\sqrt{x-2}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{x-3}-\sqrt{x-2}}{\sqrt{x-3}-\sqrt{x-2}} & = \\ \frac{3(\sqrt{x-3}-\sqrt{x-2})}{(\sqrt{x-3}+\sqrt{x-2})(\sqrt{x-3}-\sqrt{x-2})} & = \\ \frac{3(\sqrt{x-3}-\sqrt{x-2})}{(\sqrt{x-3})^{2}-(\sqrt{x-2})^{2}} & = \\ \frac{3(\sqrt{x-3}-\sqrt{x-2})}{x-3-(x-2)} & = \\ \frac{3(\sqrt{x-3}-\sqrt{x-2})}{-1} & = \\ 3\sqrt{x-2}-3\sqrt{x-3}\end{aligned}
$$
